Scripting Syntax Overview
This module discusses the scripting language which is provided as a
customization tool, extensibility tool kit and also its syntax .
Scripting is a programming language that Finacle supports for various
events. Scripting also allows formatting account numbers between
Finacle and allied products like ATM, IBR and so on. The scripts for
formatting account number across products and scripts for preload
forms are pre-defined. All the scripts must exist at predefined
locations. The users can only alter scripts as per their requirements.
As any other programming language, scripting has its own syntax.
Scripting can use certain variables, available from certain memory
areas called as repositories. The user can within the script access the
variables from the repositories.
Scripts also have built-in functions known as user hooks. Using user
hooks the user performs the required tasks.

Technical Terms
The technical terms relevant in the context of scripting syntax are as
follows:
Repository Manager
This module provides the capability of storing variable values and
identifying these variables by a name.  This module is used by the
script engine to store values and transfer them between menu options.
The structure of a repository field reference is as follows:
[Repository Name].[Class Name].[Field Name]
Queue Table
This is the area where uncompleted workflow is stored temporarily,
until retrieved for further processing. On completion of the workflow,
the stored data is deleted and an audit record is created optionally.
TBA_SCRIPTS
TBA_SCRIPTS is an environment variable set in the commonenv file.
This is the directory where all the scripts should exist. The application
will look for this directory

. If the script is not
available in this directory, it will pick the script from the directory
$TBA_PROD_ROOT/prodbase/INFENG/scripts
. If the script is also
not available in this directory also, the default logic (if available) will be
applied as specified in each case.

About Scripting
Scripting is a programming language supported by Finacle for
manipulating a set of defined input data in a script and give a defined
output data for further processing. This provides more flexibility to the
end user in manipulating the data entered in the front end to suit the
needs before the back end processes it.  Scripting is also used to
solve the usability issues in the user interface and for interfacing with
other delivery channels.
For Example:
Account numbers can be defined according to the Bank’s
requirement. The format defined can be made common for all
the accounts in the Service Outlet. In this case, the user may
not want to enter the common portion of characters every time
when account number field is to be entered.
Using Finacle Scripting, it is possible for the bank to get the
common portion appended to the account number irrespective
of the menu option being executed. It can be the Bank code,
Branch code, Currency code, currency alias, Data center, etc.,
which are common to all accounts.
The account number available in the database might be in the
format 01-02-03-04-0001:
Where 01 - corresponds to Bank code, 02 - corresponds to
Branch code, 03 - corresponds to the currency alias, 04 -
corresponds to the scheme code and 0001- is the actual
account number.
If this account number has to match, the value entered in the
front end by the user, then he has to type it in the same order

 which is very cumbersome.  
To make this easier, the user will type the account number
without the ‘-‘ symbol and using scripts the account number can
be changed to a format acceptable by the backend.
For Example:
The branch may be connected to an ATM that supports only 10
character account number and the actual account number size
in Finacle may be more. In this case, the Finacle account
number format is to be converted to ATM account number
format using some logic. This can be done in scripting. The
bank will decide on the logic to derive the unique account
number for ATM from Finacle format and codes the same in the
script.
The account number in Finacle may be 01-02-03-04-0001.
Where 01 - corresponds to Bank code 02 - corresponds to
Branch code 03 - corresponds to the currency alias 04 -
corresponds to the scheme code 0001 is the actual account
number.
To convert to 10 character ATM account number format, the
bank may decide to leave out the bank code portion as the ATM
is attached to the branches of the same BANK and leave out the
formatting of account number with ‘-‘.
The ATM account number that is derived can be 0203040001
that must be unique in the data center.

Repositories and Classes
Scripting implements a way of passing data between the Finacle
programs, user hooks, user routines, user executables and the script
using repositories.  
A Repository is a named entity, which holds a set of named Classes.
A Class is a set of name, value pairs. The name, value pair is called a
fieldname and fieldvalue. A Class can hold only one type of fieldvalue,
which is specified during Class creation.
Integer, Float, Double, Character and String Classes are currently
supported. A fieldvalue is referenced using the syntax: Repository-
name.Class-name.Field-name
Some standard repositories and classes are managed by Finacle and
are available for use.
See 
Appendix
 for a list of repositories, classes and variables available.
The bank can also create its own repositories, classes and fields while
implementing the scripting logic. However, it is their responsibility to
cleanup these repositories after use. Else, they may occupy memory
unnecessarily.
The INPUT CLASS and OUTPUT CLASS contain fields specific to the
events.

Scripting Syntax
Every script must begin with a ‘<--start’ and end with a ‘end-->’ tag.
Script has 26 built-in scratch pad variables. These are sv_a, sv_b, …
sv_z.
All these variables are globally accessible across scripts. The user
need not define the scratch pad variables to be of a particular type.
The assignment to a scratchpad variable will decide the type of the
variable based on the type of the right-hand side. Scripting allows the
dynamic type change.
Local Variables:
Script has local variables whose scope is limited within the script and
not automatically reflected to the called scripts.
The name for local variables is prefixed by “lv_” and is ended by any
single alphabet. Hence, maximum 26 local variables can be used in a
particular script. For example lv_a through lv_z.
The scratch pad variables declared in the calling scripts are visible
and accessed in the called script whereas local variables cannot be
accessed in the called script.
This type is maintained until a new assignment is made. So Scripting
allows the dynamic type change.
For Example:
sv_a = 12.45

makes the type of 'sv_a' to be set to DOUBLE type at the first
line. Until the last line sv_a carries its type as DOUBLE. In the

Note:
1
. 
Ensure that the first line of the script is the start tag. Though this is
not essential, it helps in debugging scripts when errors are
encountered as script counts line numbers from the start tag. It is
recommended to have all comments after the start tag only.
2
. 
Start tag is mandatory but end tag is not. Its always recommended
to have end tag as well.

Expressions and Control Structures
In scripting, expressions are valid combinations of variables, literals
and operators.
Scripting provides the following control structures:
Checking a condition:
* IF (condition) THEN
statements
ENDIF
* IF (condition) THEN
statements
ELSE
statements
ENDIF
These two statements can be used depending on the necessity.
Nested IF conditions are allowed and the execution of these
statements depends on the outer loop condition.
<--start
sv_a = 10
sv_b = 12
if (sv_a > sv_b) then

Goto and Gosub
Transfer of control from one part of the script to another in the same
script file is facilitated by two constructs provided in the scripting. The
two constructs are GOTO and GOSUB.
The syntax is as follows:
GOTO LabelName
GOSUB LabelName
The LABEL referred by LabelName in GOTO statement can only be
forward referenced, GOTO cannot reference a label that exists before
this statement in the script.
In case of GOTO the execution of the script starts from the statement
where the LABEL is declared.
The LABEL referred by LabelName in GOSUB statement can be
anywhere in the script. The label can be either before or after this
GOSUB statement
In case of GOSUB the execution of the script starts from the
statement, where the LABEL is declared and returns back to the next
statement after the GOSUB as soon as it finds RETURN statement in
the script.
Note:
GOSUB cannot be used inside the control structure to point to a
SUBROUTINE that is outside the innermost control structure.

Calling and Starting another Script
Transfer of control from one script to another is facilitated by two
constructs provided in the Scripting. The two constructs are CALL and
START.
The syntax is:
CALL ( ScriptName )
START ( ScriptName )
where ScriptName is either a string, like, “ script1.scr ”, or Repository
variable or Scratchpad variables of STRING type.
In both the above statements, if the script file does not exist in the
PATH, an error is reported.
CALL ( Path, ScriptName )
START ( Path, ScriptName )
where Path is either a string or a Repository variable or scratchpad
variable of STRING type,
ScriptName is either a string or a REP variable or scratchpad variable
of STRING type
Path and ScriptName are appended to get the full path.
If the script file exists and is readable, the execution of the file starts
from the beginning.
In case of CALL the execution of the script returns back to the same

All the scratchpad variables have a global context. That is, all the

called script and vice-versa.
In case of  START the execution of the script moves from the first
script to the second and stops after the execution of the second script.

Executing User Routines
The scripting language provides the user with a facility to call user
routines, user hooks and user executables from within the script.
User routines are written and compiled into a DLL/so. Default DLL/so
is SERTN.DLL.
The following is the syntax for specifying the name of the DLL/so
within a script:
LIBNAME lib
where  lib is the name of the DLL/so  which must be in the PATH. In
UNIX, the environment variable LD_LIBRARY_PATH has to be
modified to have the path in which the “so” is present.
The following is the syntax for calling a user routine within a script:
sv_a = URTN_FunctionName ( STRING )
where  sv_a will have the value returned from the function
FunctionName,
FunctionName  is the function that exists in the lib and
STRING is either a string, like, “Data”, or a REP variable or
scratchpad variable of STRING type.
The interface for the user routines is
int UserRtn ( IW_WEB_EXE_ENV_PTR WExeEnvPtr, void *
SEHandle, char * InBuff, char ** OutBuff, int * iLen, int * iRet)

Executing User Executables
User executables are used to execute other executables, read the
data dumped by them and populate the appropriate Rep, Class and
Fields.
The following is the syntax for calling a User Executable within a
script:
sv_a = UREX ( ExecutableName, ReturnDataFile, Arg )
where  sv_a will have the exit value of the Executable,
ExecutableName,
ExecutableName is the Executable’s name and is either a string, like
“Data”, or a REP variable or scratchpad variable of STRING type
ReturnDataFile is the file in which the ExecutableName dumps all the
return data. It is either a string, like “Data”, or a REP variable or
scratch pad variable of STRING type.
Arg is the argument that is passed to the ExecutableName. It is either
a string, like, “Data”, or a REP variable or scratchpad variable of
STRING type.
The ExecutableName is called with two parameters. First argument is
ReturnDataFile while the second is Arg.
The exit  value of the ExecutableName is returned in the left hand
variable, in this case sv_a. The following exit values are reserved by
the Script Engine :
35:
Ip address : 10.11.32.16 User Name:Rejith Krishnan       Time Stamp : 6/17/2025 11:20:12 PMFinacle Copyright
250 ( SE_EXEC_FAILED) - Exec failed
251 ( SE_EXEC_GAVE_CORE) - Executed process gave a core
252 ( SE_EXEC_STOPPED) - Executed process stopped
The ExecutableName dumps all the return data in
REP.CLASS.FIELD=VALUE format separated by (‘\ n’ or ‘\ t’ or ‘ ‘) in
the file ReturnDataFile. The Script Engine parses the file
ReturnDataFile  and populates the appropriate Repositories with the
data. The type of Repository is found according to following set of
rules :
If VALUE starts with ‘ ’ ’, then it is of type CHAR,
If VALUE starts with ‘ ” ’, then it is of type STRING and is terminated
by closing ‘ ” ‘,
If VALUE contains ‘ . ’, then it is of type DOUBLE/FLOAT. Script
Engine gets the type of the CLASS and puts the value appropriately,
Else the VALUE is of type INTEGER.
If the Repository or Class does not exist, then an error is set. The user
is supposed to create the ReturnDataFile in case it doesn’ t exist. After
parsing, ReturnDataFile is removed by the Script Engine.

Encryption and Decryption of Scripts
The script files are ASCII text files and can be looked at and even
modified at the Finacle installations. These scripts must be protected
against modifications in the installations. Hence, encryption is
provided using which the bank can write scripts and encrypt them
before putting them into live installations. Scripting automatically
detects if a file is encrypted and decrypts it if required.
Encryption/decryption utility [bauu9375]
Usage :
 bauu9375 <Input File Name> <Output File Name> <mode
E/D>
For Example:
$bauu9375 bg_issue1.scr bg_issue.scr E
where <Input File Name> is the input file to be
encrypted/decrypted,
<Output File Name> is the output file,
<mode E/D> is the mode, E (encryption) and D (decryption).
The utility warns if the user tries to encrypt a file that has already been
encrypted or tries to decrypt a file that is already decrypted.

Scripting has it own control statements and operators to validate

more flexibility for the application programmer, scripting allows the
